facts.statement: The study examined 482 adults living in the community, including 235 men and 247 women, with an average age of 67.2 years.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers measured blood levels of myostatin, muscle mass, and grip strength, and used high-resolution brain scans to look for links between myostatin and the volume of grey matter in different brain areas.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Men in the study had 17.8% higher levels of myostatin in their blood than women and were on average older.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Higher myostatin levels were associated with greater muscle mass in both men and women, but were not linked to grip strength.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: In men, higher myostatin levels were associated with larger grey matter volume in the left postcentral gyrus and smaller volume in the right cerebellum.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: In women, higher myostatin levels were associated only with smaller grey matter volume in three specific brain regions.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The brain regions where myostatin was linked to grey matter volume were completely different between men and women, with no overlap.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: This study provides the first evidence from human brain scans that the relationship between muscle and brain structure differs by sex.
facts.subject: humans
